title: A method exploiting direct communication between phasor measurement units for power system wide-area protection and control algorithms
author: Almas, Vanfretti
materials: As the last step of this method, the important outputs of the algorithms, which are trip signals or control commands, are mapped to the physical output of the PMU so that they can be accessed through PMUs’ digital inputs/outputs (I/Os). Furthermore, these important algorithm outputs are mapped to the front panel LEDs of the PMU to give an instant indication of the alarm situation and operational state of the algorithm executed. It is also possible to map the output of the algorithm as IEC 61850-8-1 GOOSE message [6], [7]. Furthermore, the additional delay can result in false activation of the back-up protections which may result in cascading failures leading to blackout. In case of synchrophasor-assisted control applications such as power oscillation damping, this delay in the feedback loop can degrade the performance of oscillation damping controller or incorporate negative damping into the system [20].

steps.title: Connect RTS analog outputs to PMU inputs
steps.instruction: Connect the three‑phase voltage and current analog outputs of the Opal‑RT eMEGAsim real‑time simulator to the current transformer (CT) and voltage transformer (VT) inputs of PMU‑A (remote) and PMU‑B (local) using linear amplifiers that raise the simulator’s low‑level signals (±10 V and ±20 mA) to the PMU‑compatible levels (≈100 V and 1 A).

steps.title: Configure PMU‑A and PMU‑B synchrophasor settings
steps.instruction: Using the SEL AcSELerator Quickset software, set PMU‑A to compute synchrophasors for voltage phases A, B, C and the positive‑sequence voltage of Bus 2; set PMU‑B to compute synchrophasors for voltage phases A, B, C and the positive‑sequence voltage of Bus 1. Enable Port 1 on PMU‑A and Port 2 on PMU‑B for IEEE C37.118.2 synchrophasor protocol communication.

steps.title: Make PMU‑B a client of PMU‑A
steps.instruction: In the communication settings of PMU‑B, configure it to operate as a client that receives synchrophasor streams from PMU‑A on the selected port at the required data rate; keep PMU‑A in its normal server mode.

steps.title: Parse and map remote synchrophasors
steps.instruction: When the client connection is active, PMU‑B receives the remote synchrophasor stream from PMU‑A, parses each magnitude‑angle (or real‑imaginary) pair, and maps them to local analog variables: one variable for magnitude/real part and one for angle/imaginary part. Also map the remote frequency/ROCOF to a local analog variable and remote Boolean status flags to local digital variables (e.g., RTCAP01 ← remote positive‑sequence magnitude 0.998 kV, RTCAP02 ← remote angle 76.492°).

steps.title: Deploy anti‑islanding logic in PMU‑B
steps.instruction: Create protection‑logic equations in PMU‑B that compute the phase‑angle difference between the local positive‑sequence voltage and the mapped remote positive‑sequence voltage. If the absolute difference exceeds 15° for more than 10 cycles (≈200 ms), trigger the timer PCT01 and, upon timer expiry, generate a trip signal (PSV02).

steps.title: Map algorithm outputs to PMU I/Os and LEDs
steps.instruction: Assign the trip signal and alarm status produced by the logic to PMU‑B’s physical digital outputs, front‑panel LEDs, and Human‑Machine Interface. Also configure the same status to be sent as an IEC 61850‑8‑1 GOOSE message (e.g., PSV02) through the Ethernet port.

steps.title: Configure RTS to receive GOOSE message
steps.instruction: In the Opal‑RT real‑time simulator, add a “GOOSE Subscriber” block, set its parameters as shown in Fig. 11b, and connect its binary output (0 = normal, 1 = trip) to the control input of circuit breaker CB‑1 so that a received trip command opens the breaker and disconnects the generator.

steps.title: Run RT‑HIL simulation and create island
steps.instruction: Compile the MATLAB/Simulink model of the single‑generator system (including local load) for real‑time execution. Start the simulation, and at t = 10 s open circuit breakers CB‑2a and CB‑2b to isolate the generator and its load, creating an island with a 5 % active‑power mismatch.

steps.title: Observe protection response and timing
steps.instruction: Monitor the phase‑angle difference; it will exceed 15° at ≈10.86 s, start the 10‑cycle timer, and generate the trip signal at ≈11.06 s (1.06 s after islanding). Verify that the trip signal is reflected on PMU‑B’s digital output, front‑panel LEDs, and that the GOOSE message causes CB‑1 to open. Confirm that the total response time is well within the IEEE Std 1547‑2008 2 s requirement.

description: For the specific case of synchrophasor-based Wide Area Protection and Control (WAP&C) applications, synchrophasors from two Phasor Measurement Units (PMUs) may be sufficient to perform protection and control actions [1], [2]. This method proposes the use of direct communication between two PMUs to deploy WAP&C applications. This eliminates the requirement of an intermediate Phasor Data Concentrator (PDC) and protocol parser, thus avoiding the non-deterministic delays incurred by these processes. This method utilizes both local and remote synchrophasor measurements internally in a PMU to execute WAP&C algorithms. These algorithms are deployed using protection logic equations [3], which are supported by most PMU vendors. The outputs of the algorithms (e.g. trip or control command) are mapped to the outputs and front panel of the PMU. As these WAP&C utilizes resources of the PMUs, their deployment does not require any additional external hardware controller. Thus the overall time for WAP&C application prototyping is reduced and its deployment cost is curtailed. This method is based on direct relay-to-relay communication that is used in the field of power system protection for achieving fast tripping, deploying tele-protection schemes and for monitoring status of remote protection relays [4]. The authors, in this method, propose using a similar method for PMUs to deploy protection and control applications. The method described in the previous section is illustrated and validated by coupling commercial PMUs from Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories (SEL) [8] as Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) with Opal-RT’s eMEGAsim Real-Time Simulator (RTS) [9] and analysing an anti-islanding protection scheme [1]. This type of simulation is termed as Real-Time Hardware-in-the-Loop (RT-HIL) simulation [10].
